findings.title: Pin and verify the fetched installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image rebuild downloads and executes mutable content outside the repository with no version pin or checksum/signature verification. A compromised host, changed script, or intercepted response can execute arbitrary commands during the image build without a source change.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline reports sh's exit status, not curl's. A transport failure can leave sh with empty input, which exits successfully; the image is then built without the intended installation and the failure is silently lost.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever bytes the URL serves during every build, without a version pin or integrity check. A compromised endpoint, DNS/proxy alteration, or changed upstream script receives shell execution in the image build environment.

findings.title: Fail the build when fetching the installer fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline returns sh's exit status rather than curl's. If curl has a transport failure and writes no script, sh receives empty input and exits successfully, so the Docker layer can succeed without installing the required dependency. curl also lacks -f, so HTTP error responses are not treated as fetch failures.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build fetches and executes whatever bytes example.com serves at that moment. A compromised origin, DNS path, or changed installer can run arbitrary code during CI/image builds and silently alter the produced image.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported function discards that error and returns "", making an absent key indistinguishable from a present key whose stored value is legitimately empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for absent keys, but this exported wrapper discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a failed lookup from a legitimate empty string.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key at src/store.go:10, but this exported API discards that error and returns "". A caller cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose legitimate value is "", so it can act on missing data as real data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every value was sent. It now returns immediately after scheduling goroutines, so a caller that closes results after Run returns can race with a goroutine send and panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot rely on all results being available on return.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job's send now runs in a detached goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that treats Run returning as producer completion may close the results channel, causing an asynchronous send-on-closed-channel panic; detached sends can also remain blocked indefinitely without a receiver.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every j*2 value had been sent. The new goroutines let it return immediately; a caller may close results or begin consuming a subsequent batch after Run returns, causing sends on a closed channel or results that arrive after the operation was reported complete.

findings.title: Emit the supplied log tag
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Log signature now advertises a tag argument, but the implementation ignores it and prints only message. Callers passing a tag cannot produce tagged logs, so the public API's observable behavior does not match its parameter contract.

findings.title: Restore admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With isAdmin=false and matching tenant IDs, the new OR expression returns true, authorizing a non-admin to delete a record. The prior predicate required both tenant isolation and admin privilege.

findings.title: Require same-tenant admins to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: With `||`, a non-admin session for tenant `t1` can delete any record in `t1`; an admin from `t2` can also delete a `t1` record. The prior predicate required both administrative privilege and tenant isolation.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership to delete
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing && with || authorizes deletion when either condition alone is true. A non-admin user in the record's tenant can now delete it, and an admin from a different tenant can delete another tenant's record; both were rejected by the previous authorization check.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings failures before saving updates
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid input used to throw, preventing updateFontSize from calling save. It now becomes the default settings object; updateFontSize then overwrites the stored value with {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, silently masking the error and discarding the prior theme/data.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed JSON or an invalid settings shape now returns defaults as though parsing succeeded. updateFontSize then changes the default font size and saves it, replacing the invalid persisted value; previously the parse error reached updateFontSize and prevented save from running.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or partially invalid settings now become a valid-looking default object. updateFontSize then changes its font size and saves it, so input such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"bad"} silently overwrites the user's recoverable dark-theme preference with theme "light"; previously the error stopped the write.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch and verified resolve to different commits, builtFrom reports build.ref(branch) but artifacts are returned from build.ref("verified"). Consumers receive a self-inconsistent report and can publish or inspect artifacts for the wrong build.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` reports the commit resolved from the caller-provided branch, but `artifacts` are fetched from the separate `verified` ref. For any branch whose ref differs from `verified`, the report combines metadata and artifacts from different builds.

findings.title: Use the reported branch commit for artifact lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` resolves to a different commit than `verified`, `builtFrom` reports the branch commit but `artifacts` are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-inconsistent report and can attribute verified artifacts to the wrong build.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning the feed
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. The in-repo renderFeed caller passes 20, then copies every returned item into a nominally 20-slot array; assignments beyond index 19 extend that array, so feeds with more than 20 entries are returned unbounded.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit. In particular, renderFeed calls it with 20 and then writes every returned item into its nominal 20-entry output array, so inputs longer than 20 now produce feeds longer than 20.

findings.title: Apply the requested positive limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, recentEntries now returns every entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20, so inputs longer than 20 produce an output longer than 20 despite its fixed page allocation.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but the header still receives entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry therefore declares `# entry-count: 2` while containing only one entry row, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse row count.

findings.title: Report the number of emitted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering removes stale entries from the rendered rows, but the unchanged `# entry-count` header still receives `entries.length`. Consumers parsing the header will expect more data rows than the manifest contains.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry has stale=true, it is removed from the output rows but `headerLines` still receives `entries.length`. The emitted `# entry-count` therefore exceeds the number of manifest records, producing an internally inconsistent manifest for consumers that use the header to parse or validate it.

findings.title: Preserve the legacy ID formatter API
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package API. Removing it makes any downstream consumer that still formats persisted or interoperating LEG identifiers fail to compile when upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported ids.FormatLegacyID is a source-incompatible API change. Any downstream consumer that upgrades while still formatting persisted or interoperable legacy IDs will fail to compile, with no replacement or deprecation path.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module and is removed without a compatibility export. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, even though quoteShipping preserves its calculation.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was exported from src/orders.ts and is now absent. Existing consumers importing it from this module fail to compile or load after upgrade; the new quoteShipping export lives at a different module path and does not preserve that contract.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was exported from this module before this change, but is now removed. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Return a denial for incompatible stored hash values
findings.whyItBreaks: compare_digest raises TypeError when stored_hash is bytes or a non-ASCII str, whereas the previous equality returned false and guard returned 401. A malformed persisted/configured hash can therefore turn an authentication failure into an unhandled error.

findings.title: Restore execute's successful result path
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute function now throws "always fails"; callers can no longer receive the string result previously produced from input.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation of the exported execute function now throws "always fails"; no caller can receive the string return value provided by the prior implementation.

findings.title: Restore execute's result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute API now throws before producing its promised string result; previously execute('abc') returned 'ABC'.

findings.title: Keep active viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only". The new role rejection returns "rejected" first, making handle's viewer branch unreachable.

findings.title: Keep eligible viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. This bypasses the explicit viewer "read-only" result at line 25, which was reachable before this change.

findings.title: Keep active viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only". This new guard rejects that same request before handle reaches its dedicated viewer branch, making the read-only action unreachable.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; therefore a normal `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` order now returns `"blocked"` instead of `"saved"`. Payment may govern submission, but it should not prevent persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep payment validation out of draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, the new predicate returns false, so `saveDraft` returns "blocked". Saving a draft must remain possible before payment; payment legitimately governs submission, not draft persistence.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; therefore a draft with `payment: "missing"` now returns `"blocked"` instead of `"saved"`. Saving an unpaid draft is independently legitimate and was allowed before this change.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the selected channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies the channel head while Snapshot.files describes stable. Consumers therefore publish an internally inconsistent snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the selected channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's commit while Snapshot.files contains stable's tree. Consumers therefore publish or inspect mismatched revision metadata and content.

findings.title: Load files from the published channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports that channel's commit but contains stable's file list. Consumers cannot reconstruct or trust the advertised snapshot revision.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build("x", 3) still returns 10 items because the loop uses a hard-coded max_count instead of limit. The public parameter name promises that it controls the result bound.

findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The removed fallback previously converted that supported condition to workers=1; startup now evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError instead of starting.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and then returns nil. This exported API therefore makes failed charges indistinguishable from successful ones, allowing callers to treat a rejected payment as completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers of this exported API therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a successful one and may continue as though payment completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A failed Gateway.Submit is logged but Charge returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish a declined/failed payment from a completed charge.

findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads setting `name`, a read of the same `name` for tenant B returns tenant A's cached value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`. The previous key included `tenantId`; this change makes settings incorrect across tenants.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(1) now returns 2,000 milliseconds, and schedulePoll was updated to consume that value directly. retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), so its second retry waits 2,000,000 ms (~33 minutes) instead of 2 seconds; capped retries wait about 8.3 hours.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1,000 before setTimeout. A first failed retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) rather than 1,000 ms; higher attempts can wait up to 30,000,000 ms.

findings.title: Remove the stale seconds-to-milliseconds conversion in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). After one failed attempt it waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30 minutes instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Return errors from closing the saved file
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() discards its returned error. Previously, a successful flush returned f.Close()'s error to callers; now Save returns nil when finalization fails, so callers cannot detect a failed save.

findings.title: Propagate the final file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. After a successful Flush, Save returns nil even if Close reports a finalization/write error; before this change, that error was returned to the caller.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing the returned f.Close() result with defer f.Close() discards a close failure. Callers of exported Save can now receive nil even when final file close fails, conflating an unsuccessful save with success.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is exclusive, but `range(start, end - 1)` also excludes its final value. Thus each page drops its last row; with `page_size=1`, every rendered page is empty. `summarize` consumes this output and returns incomplete page contents.

findings.title: Include the page end position
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds helper returns end as the exclusive index, but range(start, end - 1) stops one position earlier. A one-row page returns no rows; otherwise each page loses its last row. render_page and summarize therefore produce incomplete output.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint in the iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is an exclusive bound, but `range(start, end - 1)` also excludes `end - 1`. Thus every non-empty page omits its last row; pages of size one render empty, and `render_page`/`summarize` publish incomplete results.

findings.title: Preserve the public keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: The public functions renamed accepted parameters (`n`/`lo`/`hi`, `total`/`size`, and `page`/`size`). Existing callers using the prior documented-by-signature keyword form, such as `page_window(rows, page=0, size=10)`, now fail with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument`.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice jobs while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the next index. Thus adjacent completed jobs remain: `[{done:true}, {done:true}]` returns one completed job instead of none. This also changes the exported function's prior non-mutating behavior by altering the caller's array.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Once its TTL has elapsed, the cache instead returns the stale entry without deleting it.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: `forEach` advances its index after `splice` shifts the array. For adjacent completed jobs, such as `[done, done]`, removing index 0 shifts the second job to index 0, then iteration advances to index 1 and leaves that completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return cache entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so it fails `> this.ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned indefinitely rather than expiring.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into its index, but `forEach` then advances to the following index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job is skipped and returned. This also changes the prior public behavior by mutating the caller's array.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average value
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty rows array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the prior numeric result 0. Consumers can no longer safely use averageAmount as a number for empty datasets.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Previously busiest sorted a copy, so callers retained their original row ordering; this change silently reorders their input.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows=[], reduce returns 0 and division by rows.length yields NaN. The prior implementation returned 0, so consumers can no longer use the exported function's numeric result for empty datasets.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's rows in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates `rows`. Calling `busiest` now silently reorders the caller's input, unlike the prior defensive-copy implementation; callers that retain display, insertion, or processing order will observe changed data after a read-only-looking lookup.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: For [], reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the prior numeric result 0. Consumers of the number result can propagate NaN into calculations or displayed statistics.

findings.title: Do not sort the caller's rows array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates `rows`. Previously, busiest ranked a copy, so callers could safely retain their input order. This change silently reorders caller-owned data after selecting the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For scores 9, 10, and 2 with n=1, rankScores produces [9, 2, 10], so topPlayers uses 9 as the cutoff and returns the 9-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Sort numeric scores with a numeric comparator
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts score numbers as strings. With input scores [10, 2, 9] and n=2, rankScores returns [9, 2, 10], making the cutoff 2; topPlayers then returns the first two input players (10 and 2), incorrectly excluding score 9.

findings.title: Sort scores with a numeric comparator
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders score values as strings. For players ordered as 9, 100, 80 with n=1, rankScores returns [9, 80, 100], so cutoff becomes 9 and topPlayers returns the first player with score 9 instead of the player with score 100.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return sooner for a mismatching prefix, exposing a timing side channel to an attacker submitting chosen signatures. The previous hmac.compare_digest implementation avoids this leakage.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == compares signatures with timing that can vary by matching prefix. An attacker able to send repeated webhook requests can use those differences to progressively forge a valid HMAC and reach processor(payload) without knowing the secret.

findings.title: Restore a constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality can return after the first mismatched character, exposing comparison timing to an attacker submitting chosen signatures. The prior hmac.compare_digest implementation avoided this oracle before handle authorized processor execution.

findings.title: Keep all transfer writes inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger row commits when the transaction exits at line 23. If either subsequent balance update fails, the transfer raises after recording a completed ledger entry; if the second update fails, the source debit may also persist without the destination credit. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after recording the ledger entry. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the transfer raises after its ledger record has already been committed; if the debit succeeds and credit fails, balances can also be left inconsistent. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the with block exits before either balance update runs. If either update raises, the transfer leaves a committed ledger entry with no balance changes, or with only the debit applied, violating transfer atomicity.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly derived all fields in UTC. The new local-time getters classify the same instant differently by server timezone; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This shifts billing boundaries and makes results depend on deployment configuration.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation produced a timezone-independent UTC billing date. This now uses the server's local timezone: for example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31. Consequently sameBillingDay can classify two different UTC billing days as equal (or vice versa) depending on where the process runs.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing date
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly generated a UTC calendar date. The new local-time getters produce a different key around UTC midnight; for example, 2026-09-06T00:30:00Z becomes 2026-09-05 in America/Los_Angeles. Billing records for the same instant will therefore be assigned to different days depending on the process timezone.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account identifier now share one memo entry. After tenant A reads account X, a read for tenant B/account X returns A's cached Profile and skips fetchProfile, exposing the wrong tenant's profile data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two requests for the same account under different tenants now share one cache entry. After tenant A's profile is cached, readProfile(tenantB, account, ...) returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing the wrong tenant's data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After fetching tenant A's account X, a read for tenant B's account X uses the same `account` key and returns A's cached Profile without calling `fetchProfile`. The returned object explicitly carries its tenant, so this produces a wrong cross-tenant result.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`, but now returns `""`. Callers, including loadAll, cannot distinguish an absent value from a deliberately stored empty string and may process incomplete data as valid.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is a valid stored value. `loadAll` consequently returns arrays containing indistinguishable fallback values instead of failing, so callers cannot detect incomplete loads.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts the deliberate `missing: <key>` error into `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking successful results containing empty values instead of reporting a missing key.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported interface removes required `timeoutMs` and adds required `retries`/`timeout`. Any existing consumer using the prior documented shape, such as `{ maxAttempts: 3, timeoutMs: 1000 }`, fails TypeScript checking after upgrade before retry can run.

findings.title: Expose failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from the public `retryBackground` callback is discarded, and deadline expiry or retry exhaustion returns the same `void` result as success. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background operation from one that never succeeded and may treat the failed work as complete.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for timeoutMs configurations
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers pass Config objects with timeoutMs. After this change, config.timeout is undefined; Date.now() + undefined is NaN, so the deadline guard at line 10 never expires and retry runs every maxAttempts attempt instead of honoring the configured timeout. TypeScript callers also fail because timeoutMs is no longer accepted and new required retries is missing.

findings.title: Report exhausted retryBackground failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When every fn invocation throws, retryBackground catches each exception and returns void after the loop. Its caller cannot distinguish an eventual success from total failure, so it can proceed as though the background operation completed.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields during the rename
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers construct Config with `maxAttempts` and `timeoutMs`. They now fail type checking because both required `retries` and `timeout` are missing. Untyped callers pass `undefined` for `timeout`; `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN, so the deadline guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Make retryBackground asynchronous or rename it
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` invokes `fn()` synchronously in its caller's stack and does not return until success, exhaustion, or the deadline. The exported name promises background execution, but the implementation is a synchronous duplicate of `retry` with a different attempt field.

findings.title: Expose terminal retry failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is discarded, and exhaustion/deadline returns `void`, exactly like success. Because this is a newly exported API, every caller is forced to treat a failed operation as indistinguishable from a successful one.

findings.title: Support numeric values before accepting them
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now permits a number, but `value.length` is invalid for numbers. TypeScript rejects this implementation, and even non-typechecked execution would produce `len=undefined` for numeric input.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading `length`
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now accepts `number`, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript reports an error for `value.length`, preventing a typechecked build; if emitted without checking, numeric input renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `value` now permits `number`, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this component, preventing a typed build; if emitted without type checking, numeric values render as `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. A PR with a diff larger than that makes the git diff call at line 140 fail before the review try/catch, so Needlefish posts no review or failure check. The prior 64 MiB limit supported these PRs.

findings.title: Restore capacity for full PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: This helper produces the complete review patch at line 140. Removing its 64 MiB maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's 1 MiB default; a PR diff exceeding that size terminates the git child with ENOBUFS and the review fails instead of submitting a result. The previous implementation explicitly supported these patches.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff` at line 140 now uses `spawnSync`'s default 1 MiB `maxBuffer` rather than the prior 64 MiB limit. A PR with a larger textual diff makes `spawnSync` fail before review generation, so the GitHub review action cannot review that PR.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review subprocesses
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex executes model-provided commands with opts.repoPath as its working directory. Removing the explicit `-s read-only` allows the CLI's configured/default sandbox policy to grant write access, so a review prompt or compromised model response can modify the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets the Codex process invoked with an arbitrary review prompt operate without this wrapper's explicit no-write restriction while its working directory is the reviewed repository. A prompt-injected or erroneous agent action can now alter repository files, undermining the review-only boundary.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex executes a caller-provided prompt in opts.repoPath. Removing -s read-only delegates sandbox selection to Codex configuration/defaults, so a workspace-write or danger-full-access configuration can let hostile repository content or a prompt modify the repository during a supposedly local review.

findings.title: Use the merge base for the reviewed diff
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be a newer base-branch tip that is not an ancestor of the PR checkout/HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then reports base-only commits as removals or changes, so the review bundle and inline-comment path set include code not authored by the PR. The prior merge-base calculation avoided this by comparing the PR head only against its common ancestor with the base.

findings.title: Restore merge-base comparison for PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip rather than an ancestor of the PR head, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes commits made only on the base branch as apparent deletions. The review bundle can therefore contain unrelated changes and produce invalid review findings/comments.

findings.title: Build the review range from the PR merge base and head
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be ahead of the PR branch's fork point. Diffing it directly against HEAD includes base-only commits as reverse changes, so review() receives a patch and changed-file list that do not represent the PR. These lines also ignore PR_HEAD_SHA even though that SHA is retained in the bundle and used when posting the review; when checkout HEAD differs from the configured PR head, findings are generated for one commit and submitted against another.

findings.title: Keep prompt replacement values literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. bundle.patch is included in the JSON inserted at line 25 and is directly inserted at line 33, so a reviewed patch containing (for example) "$&" is changed into the placeholder text rather than preserved. This silently corrupts the candidate and critic prompts; the same issue can also corrupt model findings inserted at line 32.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences when inserting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. Bundle JSON, generated findings, and especially arbitrary diff text can legitimately contain these sequences; for example, a patch containing $& is rewritten to the placeholder text rather than passed literally to Codex. This silently corrupts the review or critic prompt.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in injected prompt content
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats a string replacement as a substitution template. A patch, bundle field, or candidate finding containing `$&` is rewritten to the matched placeholder (`{{BUNDLE}}`, `{{FINDINGS}}`, or `{{PATCH}}`) instead of being delivered literally to Codex; `$`` and `$'` can also duplicate surrounding prompt text. Since bundle.patch is arbitrary reviewed source text, this corrupts the review/critic input and can cause real diff content or findings to be omitted or misread.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial POST fails and the PR receives a new commit before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's most recent commit rather than headSha, which is the commit Needlefish analyzed. This can request changes or report a pass against unreviewed code.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in fallback reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary review request fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If a new commit arrives after this run captured and reviewed headSha, the fallback can submit REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT against that newer, unreviewed commit, while its body describes the old diff.

findings.title: Keep the review bound to the analyzed commit in the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary review request fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review with the PR's current head instead of headSha that was diffed and analyzed. If new commits arrive between analysis and fallback, a stale pass or change request is applied to code Needlefish did not review.

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: A finding such as `{ "title": "x" }`, which previously raised a malformed-output error (or was omitted with `strict=false`), now becomes a P1 bug at file "" and line 0 with empty rationale and fix. `normalizeReview` returns that fabricated record to consumers, so they cannot distinguish invalid model output from a real finding. Removing the exported `strict` parameter also breaks TypeScript consumers calling `normalizeReview(raw, false)`.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid model output that previously raised a malformed-review error is now converted into a seemingly valid finding (for example, invalid severity becomes P1 and missing locations become line 0). As an exported normalization API, this forces callers to conflate invalid output with a real review result.

findings.title: Trim category values before validating them
findings.whyItBreaks: A category such as " security " was accepted and normalized to "security" before this change. It now fails CATEGORIES.includes and is silently reclassified as "bug", producing an incorrect finding category.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid model output that previously aborted normalization, such as severity "BAD" or a missing file/lineStart, is now returned as a P1 bug at file "" and line 0. Callers can no longer distinguish malformed review output from a genuine finding and may render or act on an unaddressable false finding.

findings.title: Keep explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any checkout. `gh pr view` without `-R` resolves a repository from the current Git repository, but this workflow has not established one yet. Manual runs therefore cannot resolve the requested PR's head/base SHAs and abort before review.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow_dispatch path enters this branch before any checkout. Without `-R "$REPO"` (or `GH_REPO`), `gh pr view` must infer a repository from the current directory's git remote, which is unavailable in a fresh Actions workspace. The commands fail, emit no head/base outputs, and the requested manual review cannot proceed.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout establishes a Git remote. `gh pr view <number>` therefore has no repository context after `-R "$REPO"` was removed. The refs outputs become unavailable/empty, so the workflow cannot reliably check out and review the requested PR.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid provider output (including null, missing summary, or non-array findings) is converted to a structurally valid review with an empty summary and no findings. Callers of this exported API can no longer distinguish a failed/malformed review from a legitimate review that found nothing, so they may report or persist a false clean result.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously rejected as malformed, such as null or an object missing findings, checked, or residual_risks, now produce a seemingly successful review with empty fields. Consumers cannot distinguish an invalid model/tool response from a legitimate zero-finding review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or absent review output previously threw a malformed-review error. It now becomes a valid-looking RawReview with empty summary, findings, checked, and residual_risks fields, so every public caller is forced to conflate provider/parser failure with a legitimate no-findings review.

findings.title: Restore PR-specific refs for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The fallback github.ref is the ref selected to dispatch the workflow, not the required inputs.pr_number PR head, so the self-review workflow can install and run code from main (or another selected branch) while posting results to the requested PR. The same event leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty at lines 45-46, and fetches main rather than the requested PR's actual base branch at line 35.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR ref on manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: `workflow_dispatch` has no `pull_request` payload, so the head expression falls back to `github.ref` and the base expression falls back to `main`, ignoring the required `pr_number`. Dispatching from `main` for PR N therefore checks out and reviews `main` while passing PR N to `--pr`, allowing results for unrelated code to be posted to PR N. The removed resolver previously queried PR N for its head and base refs.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event has no pull_request payload, so the first operand is empty and checkout uses github.ref—the branch selected to run the workflow—instead of the head of inputs.pr_number. The old Resolve PR refs step queried that PR and checked out its head. A manually requested PR is therefore reviewed using arbitrary/default-branch tool code rather than the requested PR checkout.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal calls git diff at line 100. Omitting maxBuffer changes spawnSync from the prior 64 MiB limit to Node's 1 MiB default; a diff between 1 MiB and 64 MiB causes ENOBUFS, leaves status null, and the status guard at line 12 throws instead of producing a review.

findings.title: Preserve the Git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. The git helper is used to collect the complete patch at line 100, so any repository diff larger than 1 MiB now terminates with a maxBuffer error before review can begin; the prior code intentionally supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the entire patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at lines 98-100. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node’s 1 MiB default and terminates Git when a textual diff exceeds it; the review then throws instead of reviewing a diff that the prior 64 MiB limit supported.

findings.title: Publish review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this posts a completed neutral check even though the review did not run. GitHub accepts neutral required checks for protected-branch merges, so a required Needlefish check no longer blocks merging on review failures.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or result publishing throws, this catch path reports the completed Needlefish check as neutral. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-status-check result, so a PR can merge even though the review did not run to completion; this contradicts the emitted message that it did not pass.

findings.title: Keep review failures failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or posting its result throws, this path still says the PR did not pass, but reports the completed check as neutral. GitHub treats neutral as successful for required checks, so a required Needlefish check no longer blocks merging after the reviewer failed to run.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out as the workspace and then its package installation and src/cli.ts are executed. A same-repository PR author can modify the CLI, package scripts, or lockfile to run arbitrary code with GITHUB_TOKEN permissions including pull-requests: write and checks: write, and can compromise the persistent self-hosted runner.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout independent of the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: After checking out the PR head, this runs `pnpm install` and `src/cli.ts` from that same untrusted checkout. A same-repository PR can modify the CLI to report success or alter its install scripts, so the required review can be bypassed; it also executes attacker-controlled code on the self-hosted runner while a token with pull-request and checks write permissions is available.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer executable on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head and directly executes its src/cli.ts while GH_TOKEN is available in this step. Same-repository PRs receive the configured pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions, so a PR can alter the reviewer to forge review/check output or use the self-hosted runner and token outside the intended review boundary.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the installed reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: At the reviewed head, the repository contains neither package.json nor src/cli.ts. After removing the frankekn/needlefish checkout, pnpm install has no project manifest and the subsequent tsx invocation targets a nonexistent file, so every review job fails before producing a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve severity canonicalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously accepted severity strings such as " p2 " or "p0" by trimming and uppercasing them. The changed exact-membership check rejects those inputs and returns P3, so a supplied high-severity finding is silently converted to the lowest severity.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external review JSON and passes each item to this function at src/shared/schema.ts:132. A severity such as "p1" or " P1 ", which previously normalized to P1, now fails the exact-match check and is returned as P3. This silently downgrades the reported priority of an otherwise recognizable finding.

findings.title: Preserve severity case and whitespace normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped JSON and passes each finding to this exported normalizer. A valid external value such as " p1 " or "p1" previously normalized to "P1" but now fails the exact-match check and is silently emitted as "P3", changing finding priority.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized `env`, `spawnSync` inherits `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The invoked Codex process and commands it launches can therefore authenticate to GitHub with the runner's credentials, despite this wrapper selecting read-only filesystem sandboxing. Prompt- or repository-influenced agent actions can now use those credentials to alter external GitHub state.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, exposing `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` to the Codex CLI and its subprocesses. The previous implementation intentionally removed these credentials, so untrusted repository/prompt-controlled Codex activity can now access CI GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN into the Codex process, where prompt-controlled tool execution can read or use them against GitHub APIs. The removed code explicitly prevented this credential exposure.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before using the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs can now enter this job, which checks out the attacker-controlled head SHA and executes attacker-controlled dependency metadata and src/cli.ts on a persistent self-hosted runner. This bypasses the prior trust boundary and permits compromise of runner-resident credentials or subsequent jobs.

findings.title: Restore the fork PR guard
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now run a checkout of attacker-controlled head code on a self-hosted runner. That code is executed during `pnpm install` and again through `tsx src/cli.ts`, allowing an external contributor to compromise or persist on the runner.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository condition causes `pull_request` events from forks to run their checked-out head, dependency installation, and CLI on the self-hosted runner. A fork author can change package metadata or source to execute arbitrary commands on that runner, compromising its credentials and persistent workspace.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration configuration values
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, a configured value of "0" was accepted and passed to setTimeout, allowing an immediate SIGKILL or immediate give-up. This change rejects 0 and silently substitutes 5000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or 2000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, changing behavior for existing valid settings.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner delay settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, an explicit environment value of "0" was accepted. It now falls back to 5000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or 2000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, so configurations requesting immediate SIGKILL escalation or immediate give-up instead wait several seconds.

findings.title: Allow explicit zero cleanup delays
findings.whyItBreaks: Both environment settings previously accepted "0" as a valid timer delay. With this change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits the 5000 ms fallback before SIGKILL instead of escalating immediately, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving instead of giving up immediately. This breaks existing configurations that intentionally require prompt cleanup.

findings.title: Restore deep review coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles retain only six mapper-selected hotspots. Previously, every changed file absent from those selected hotspots was appended to a tail hotspot and deep-reviewed. A mapper result with more than six disjoint hotspots, or one that omits a file, now silently skips those files; defects in them can reach the critic without any deep-review evidence.

findings.title: Propagate residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can return residual_risks, including blockers for unresolved material evidence. This change replaces their aggregation with an unconditional empty array before passing the candidate to the critic. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a review with deep-review blockers from one with none, and may return a non-blocking verdict despite an unresolved deep review.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large PRs select at most six mapped hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot leaves every changed file not included by those six without a deep review; the critic receives only findings and a patch stat, so it can return a clean review without examining defects in omitted files.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep pass can return residual_risks specifically when it cannot establish a safe verdict. The new candidate always replaces those signals with [], so the critic cannot distinguish an unresolved blocking risk from a fully reviewed hotspot and may emit a PASS.

findings.title: Restore deep review coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles may contain more changed surfaces than the six selected hotspots, or a mapper may omit a file. The removed tail hotspot was the only mechanism that sent those files to deep review; this loop now reviews only selected hotspots and can return a clean verdict while changed files were never inspected.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can report a blocking residual risk, but the merged candidate now replaces all of them with an empty array. The critic therefore cannot distinguish an unresolved review from a fully reviewed patch, and the final verdict can pass despite a deep reviewer explicitly reporting that it lacks required evidence.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot failures as blocked review results
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed deep-review response now rejects the entire large-review operation immediately. Previously, the other hotspots were still reviewed and the failed one was reported as a blocking residual risk, so callers received an actionable incomplete-review result instead of no result.

findings.title: Preserve focus in each large-review deep pass
findings.whyItBreaks: For PRs routed through reviewLarge, bundle.focus is no longer substituted into deep.md. A caller requesting a focused review (for example, security) therefore receives unscoped hotspot reviews, while small reviews still pass focus through the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus in large-PR deep-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-PR path no longer substitutes bundle.focus into deep.md. A caller-supplied focus directive is therefore left as the literal {{FOCUS}} template token (and is also omitted from the map bundle), so large reviews can inspect unrelated surfaces while small reviews still receive the directive through the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus in large-review deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed replacement previously interpolated bundle.focus into each deep-review prompt. Large reviews with a requested focus now leave the template focus slot uninterpolated and do not direct hotspot reviews toward the caller's stated concern, unlike small reviews which still serialize the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,500ms, this computes 0 minutes and 60 seconds, rendering "60s" instead of the previous normalized "1m 0s". For 119,500ms it renders "1m 60s" rather than "2m 0s". Stats and total durations near every minute boundary therefore regress to invalid-looking minute/second output.

findings.title: Normalize seconds after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remainder is at least 59.5 seconds, seconds rounds to 60 without carrying into minutes. For example, 119999ms renders as `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`; this affects both individual call statistics and total duration output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For a 119500 ms stat, minutes is floored to 1 while the remainder rounds to 60, so rendered review output reports "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s".

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger now returns 0, although both its exported name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Consumers can rely on this parser to exclude zero and subsequently receive an invalid value.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger now returns 0 even though its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers relying on that guarantee can receive zero where a strictly positive value is required.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor parsePositiveInteger's contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger and its unchanged error text promise a positive integer, but value "0" now returns 0. Public callers can therefore receive a value outside the stated contract and use it as a positive timeout, retry count, or similar required-positive setting.
